issues.issue: The Licensee is named as Peter A. Morton individually, yet the operative terms speak of "his or its company" (3(d)), of Licensee "and its affiliates" operating the Las Vegas Hotel (4(a)) and of sublicensees and franchisees (Section 10), leaving unclear which entities are bound. The identity of the contracting Licensee must be worked out from those later provisions rather than from the preamble.

"All confusingly similar names, marks and logos ... and derivations thereof, to the maximum extent permitted by law" is an open-ended catch-all with no fixed boundary, sitting against the enumerated specifics "Rock Cafe" and "Hard Rock". The exclusion of the Hard Rock Hotel and Casino Marks does not resolve which uses of the bare words "Hard Rock" fall on which side of the line.

The Hard Rock Hotel Marks are defined by reference to Exhibit A, but Exhibit A lists both "Hard Rock Hotel" and "Hard Rock Casino", so the definition overlaps the Hard Rock Casino Marks defined by Exhibit B in Section 1(c). The carve-out sentence does not resolve which definition governs the mark "Hard Rock Casino".

Exhibit B contains only "Hard Rock Casino", the same mark that also appears in Exhibit A defining the Hard Rock Hotel Marks under Section 1(b), so the two mark sets cannot be kept distinct. Provisions that turn on which set is being used, such as 2(b)(i), are thereby left indeterminate.

"An all-inclusive place for lodging" and "offering a variety of amenities" are undefined and set no threshold for how many or what kind of amenities are required. Whether a given lodging facility is a "Hotel" — which drives 2(b)(i) and 3(a) — cannot be determined from these words.

"A substantial source of revenue and its principal function" states no measure of substantiality and combines two different tests without saying whether both must be met. The riverboat sentence compounds this by omitting what the "substantial source of revenue" must come from.

"Part of the same 'Hard Rock' complex/development" has no boundary — no distance, ownership or common-management test — for facilities that are not immediately contiguous. Whether a separated hotel and casino form one Hotel/Casino therefore turns on an undefined term.

This defines "Hard Rock Hotel" as a Hotel operated under the Hard Rock Hotel Marks, yet 2(b)(i) forbids Licensee from using the Hard Rock Hotel Marks in any Hotel that is not a Hotel/Casino, so the defined category has no permitted application to Licensee. Clause 2(b)(vii), which speaks of "other Hard Rock Hotels" developed by Licensee, deepens the incoherence.

"Operated under the Hard Rock Hotel Marks and/or the Hard Rock Casino Marks" leaves it uncertain whether a facility using only one of the two mark sets is a Hard Rock Hotel/Casino. That matters because 2(b)(i) permits Casino Marks alone but forbids Hotel Marks alone.

The enumeration of Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos, Hard Rock Casinos and Hard Rock Cafe restaurants omits stand-alone Hard Rock Hotels, which the definition in 1(g) and clause 2(b)(vii) contemplate, so expressio unius leaves them outside "Hard Rock Facilities". The gap matters for 2(b)(vii)'s ban on selling in "any other Hard Rock Facility" and for the cooperation duties in Section 8.

The territorial description is riddled with mechanical errors — "fifty (SO) mile radius form the City Hall" — and its geographic premise is wrong on its face, since Illinois is not west of the Mississippi and Louisiana straddles it. The radius definitions also fix no method for locating the "other similarly recognized civic center structure" or for territory falling outside the state or nation named.

"Any and all services provided by Licensee in connection with or relating to the operation" of the facilities is unbounded, and "relating to" would sweep in services having only a loose connection to the licensed facilities. The clause also miscites the defined term ("Hard Rock Hotei/Casinos").

"Licensed Products" reaches only goods "bearing the Hard Rock Hotel Marks or the Hard Rock Casino Marks", so merchandise bearing the other permitted designations under 2(b)(vi)-(viii) and 6(c) — "Beach Club", "Athletic Club" and similar "Hard Rock" designations — arguably falls outside the definition. That leaves the sale restrictions in 2(b)(iv)-(v) and the quality controls in Section 4 with an uncertain reach.

"Licensor" is defined as Rank Licensing, Inc. "or its successors, assigns or transferees", yet the notice provision in Section 12 gives the Licensor's address as a different entity, Hard Rock Cafe International (DEL), Inc. Which entity holds and may enforce the Licensor's rights is therefore not settled by the definition alone.

The grant of an "exclusive license" in the Morton Territories cannot be squared with Section 3(a), which gives Licensor "the right to the use and exploitation of the Hard Rock Hotel Marks anywhere in the world for a Hotel facility that does not include a Casino", excepting only Nevada. The two provisions both purport to control use of the Hotel Marks inside the Territories.

The worldwide carve-out permitting "promotion, advertising or marketing (not including the sale of merchandise) and broadcasting of the Hard Rock Hotel/Casinos" does not define what counts as broadcasting or promotion "of" the licensed facilities. Programming or media exploitation bearing the marks but going beyond advertising the facility falls in a zone the words do not resolve.

The ban on using the Hard Rock Hotel Marks in a Hotel that is not a Hotel/Casino cannot be squared with clause 2(b)(vii), which permits Licensee to use designations "in other Hard Rock Hotels", or with the definition of "Hard Rock Hotel" in 1(g). Whether Licensee may brand a hotel without a casino is left contradicted.

"Any restaurant ... or anywhere else that is confusingly similar to a Hard Rock Cafe restaurant" is syntactically ambiguous as to whether the confusing-similarity qualifier attaches to all restaurants or only to those outside the licensed facilities. "Other types of restaurants" in the saving sentence is likewise undefined.

The clause states that Licensor "shall retain the sole right to apply" for registrations and in the next sentence that Licensor "shall consent to any request by Licensee" for such applications, and then hands preparation and filing to Licensee as agent on Licensor's failure. Whose right it is, and what triggers the fall-back agency ("reasonably likely to affect"), are left inconsistent within the clause.

"Licensed Products must always bear the geographic location where sold" does not say what form or degree of geographic identification satisfies it, and the sentence's only stated exception cross-refers to 2(b)(vii) while 2(b)(v) creates a further Internet exception. "In or contiguous to" a licensed facility is likewise undefined.

The bar on selling Internet-designated Licensed Products "in the retail establishments described in subparagraph 2(b)(iv)" and vice versa does not say whether it separates identical physical items or whole product lines and designs. The "Hard Rock Internet access kits" carve-out is an undefined term that further clouds the line.

"The other designations such as 'Beach Club' or 'Athletic Club'" is an open-ended catch-all introduced by "such as", so what other substitute designations qualify is not fixed by the enumerated examples. The permission is also qualified by "only within the confines" and "not for the sale of merchandise", phrases whose reach over marketing, signage and web use is undefined.

The clause requires logo use "only in the manner set forth in Exhibit C", but Exhibit C's own notes say the geographic designation "may be replaced with 'Beach Club' or 'Athletic Club' as designations" without the confines-only and no-merchandise limits imposed here. The exhibit and the text cannot both be given full effect.

Exhibit D and Exhibit E list the same designations ("Beach Club"/"Athletic Club"), so this clause's permanent permission to use them in other facilities cannot be squared with 2(b)(viii), which requires Licensee to "forever cease displaying such designations" after eighteen months. Which sunset governs the same words is unresolved.

This clause's eighteen-month sunset on the Exhibit E designations conflicts with clause 2(b)(vii), which permits the identical Exhibit D designations to be used indefinitely in other Hard Rock Hotels and Casinos. The two exhibits contain the same designations, so the two clauses cannot both be given effect.

Permitting "Hard Rock Riverboat" within the circle logo cannot be squared with clause 2(b)(vi), which forbids Licensee to replace the word "Hotel" or "Casino" with any other designation absent Licensor's written consent. The clause supplies no consent mechanism of its own beyond a registration request.

Licensor's reserved right to use the Hard Rock Hotel Marks "anywhere in the world for a Hotel facility that does not include a Casino", subject only to a Nevada exception, cannot be squared with the exclusive license granted to Licensee in the Morton Territories by Section 2(a). The Nevada carve-out implies Licensor may otherwise operate inside the Territories, which the grant forbids.

The covenant runs "during the Term of this Agreement or thereafter", but "Term" is capitalized and never defined, and Section 9(a) grants the license in perpetuity with no term or termination. The temporal reach of the non-challenge promise therefore rests on a term with no referent.

Goodwill inuring "to the sole benefit of Licensor" sits awkwardly with Section 9(b), which declares Licensee "solely entitled to all economic benefits" of the licensed rights. Whether goodwill built by Licensee is an economic benefit reserved to Licensee or property of Licensor is not settled by either clause.

The bar on any word that would "dominate, modify or qualify" the Marks "other than geographical designations" cannot be squared with clauses 2(b)(vi) and 2(b)(vii), which expressly permit non-geographic designations such as "Beach Club" and "Athletic Club" in the logo. The two provisions give opposite answers on the same designations.

The quality benchmark — "good quality at least as high as the quality of similar goods presently sold ... by Licensee" at the Las Vegas facility — is self-referential and fixed to an unrecorded baseline, and "equal to and commensurate with" adds no measurable standard. What quality failure would breach the clause cannot be determined from its words.

The inspection right is qualified by "reasonable access", "reasonable notice" and the absolute condition that inspection "will not cause any disruption to Licensee's business", a qualifier broad enough to swallow the right. The clause supplies no frequency, scope or dispute mechanism for these terms.

The sentence is grammatically broken — "furnish or render ... requested Licensed Services, representative samples on the premises of each Licensed Product, their labels, packaging" — so what Licensee must produce, and whether samples leave the premises, is unclear. It also fails to say whether Licensor's "approval" is a condition to sale.

"Wherever the same may be used with reasonable convenience" supplies no measurable standard for when the marks must appear on advertising. The companion duty to cause "the appropriate notice of registration" to appear assumes registrations that Exhibits A and B do not identify.

The acknowledgment that all Licensor rights to monitor and intervene and "all standards of operation set forth herein" exist "solely" for quality control could be read to limit the commercial restrictions in Section 2(b), which are not quality provisions. It cannot easily be squared with 2(b)'s territorial, merchandise and logo restrictions read as substantive bargains.

Arbitration is confined to disputes "regarding the failure of Licensee to conform to any provision of quality control as set forth herein", but the contract never identifies which provisions are quality-control provisions. "Any substantial failure ... in any respect" and the misused word "proscribed" (for prescribed) add further uncertainty about the trigger and the selection process.

The arbitrators' power to grant permanent injunctions overlaps the judicial injunction rights reserved to the parties in Section 11(a) and the court-only carve-out in 5(d), with no rule of priority. Which forum may enjoin what conduct is left unresolved between the two sections.

The exclusion of "any claims or controversies not specifically identified hereinabove" from arbitration depends entirely on what 5(a) is taken to have specifically identified, and 5(a)'s reference to "any provision of quality control as set forth herein" is itself unspecified. A mixed dispute — quality failure alleged alongside trademark validity — cannot be allocated between the two clauses.
